title: HLA Typing Resolution and Donor Matching: Allele Fields, 6 Antigens and 8/8
summary: Read the four fields of an HLA allele name, place serology, SSP, SSO, SBT and NGS on a resolution ladder, and contrast the six-antigen kidney match with 8/8 high-resolution matching and permissive DPB1 mismatches for unrelated stem-cell donors.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 50 Hits 9 (six-antigen solid-organ match), 10 (HCT matching), 13 (typing methods by resolution) and Traps 1, 3 and 5. Checked against Dehn 2019 (NMDP/CIBMTR), the WHO nomenclature reports (Marsh 2010, 2026), Geo 2024 and Gramlick 2022. Hit 10 says HLA-A mismatches have the largest impact and frames HCT as “10 of 10”; Dehn 2019 found no locus among A, B, C and DRB1 better tolerated and says DQB1 has not been shown alone to affect survival, so the lesson teaches 8/8 plus permissive DPB1 (register rv-hct-locus-impact). Trap 3 says DP was never defined serologically; DP was historically cellularly defined (DPw), but the 2026 WHO report now names serologic DPA/DPB specificities (register rv-dp-serology). Not taught as fact: graft-survival percentages (Hit 9), “single HLA-C mismatches hurt engraftment” (Hit 10), SSP as the deceased-donor method (Hit 13).

objectives: Interpret the four fields and expression suffixes of an HLA allele name.
Rank HLA typing methods by resolution and state a limitation of each.
Contrast the six-antigen kidney match with the 8/8 high-resolution unrelated-donor HCT match and the role of DPB1.

scenes.title: Two reports, two match rules
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: two HLA reports. Report 1, kidney: the deceased donor shares both HLA-A, both HLA-B and both HLA-DR antigens with the candidate (“0 of 6 mismatched”). Report 2, stem-cell transplant: an unrelated donor matches the patient everywhere except one HLA-A allele, donor A*02:01 versus patient A*02:02. Question token: “Is A*02:01 versus A*02:02 a match?”

cues.text: Two typing reports reach the HLA laboratory. The kidney donor shares all six counted antigens with the candidate: both HLA-A, both HLA-B, both HLA-DR.
The stem-cell donor matches the patient everywhere except one HLA-A allele: the donor is A star zero two, zero one; the patient is A star zero two, zero two.
Same “A2” family. Is that a match, or a mismatch?

props.label: A*02:01 vs A*02:02: match or mismatch?

scenes.title: Reading an allele name
scenes.altText: Schematic: the allele name A*02:01:01:01 with four colon-separated fields colour-coded. Field 1 (02) = allele group, usually matching the serologic antigen (A2). Field 2 (01) = specific protein: names differing here differ by at least one amino-acid-changing substitution. Field 3 = synonymous substitutions in the coding sequence (same protein). Field 4 = differences in introns or the 5′/3′ untranslated regions. Suffix card: N = null (not expressed), L = low surface expression. Note: two-field typing is what transplant guidelines call high-resolution (allele-level) typing.

cues.text: An HLA allele name has up to four fields separated by colons. The first field is the allele group, which usually lines up with the old serologic antigen, such as A2.
The second field names the specific protein. Two alleles that differ in the second field differ by at least one substitution that changes an amino acid.
The third field separates silent, synonymous changes in the coding sequence: same protein. The fourth field marks differences in introns or untranslated regions.
Suffixes describe expression: N means a null allele that makes no protein; L means low surface expression. Two-field typing is what transplant guidelines call high resolution.

props.label: Suffix N = null · L = low · 2 fields = high resolution

scenes.title: Typing methods by resolution
scenes.altText: Ladder of methods, lowest to highest resolution. Serology (cytotoxicity-based assays on viable cells): first-field, low resolution, needs viable cells. SSP and SSO (PCR with sequence-specific primers or probes): detect known motifs, low-to-intermediate resolution; SSP is quick for a few samples; neither can recognise a novel allele. SBT (Sanger sequencing of key exons): high (two-field) resolution, can reveal new alleles, but ambiguity remains when alleles differ outside the sequenced exons. NGS: whole-gene sequence, phase of heterozygous positions, more than two fields, novel alleles; but batching and a 2–3-day turnaround make it poorly suited to urgent deceased-donor typing.

cues.text: Typing methods climb a resolution ladder. Serology, the earliest method on this ladder, needs viable cells and gives first-field, low-resolution types.

Sequence-specific primers, SSP, and sequence-specific oligonucleotide probes, SSO, are PCR methods that look for known sequence motifs. They give low to intermediate resolution, and they cannot recognise an allele nobody has described.
Sequence-based typing by Sanger sequencing reads the key exons and reaches two-field resolution, though alleles that differ outside those exons can stay ambiguous.

Next-generation sequencing reads whole genes, sets the phase of heterozygous positions, goes beyond two fields and finds novel alleles. But it is batched and takes two to three days, so it is a poor fit for urgent deceased-donor typing.

scenes.title: Two different match counts
scenes.altText: Left card, kidney: the classic match grade counts HLA-A, -B and -DR, two antigens each = 6; reported as mismatches out of 6. Right card, unrelated-donor HCT (NMDP/CIBMTR 2019): high-resolution matching at HLA-A, -B, -C and -DRB1 = 8/8. Any single mismatch at these four loci lowered survival, no locus was better tolerated, and allele-level mismatches were as harmful as antigen-level ones. DPB1: mismatched in more than 80% of unrelated transplants; choose a matched or permissive T-cell-epitope mismatch. DQB1 has not been shown on its own to change survival; “10/10” adds DQB1. Hook answer: A*02:01 vs A*02:02 = second-field (protein) difference; in this invented case it is taken to lie in the antigen recognition domain, which high-resolution matching assesses → 7/8.

cues.text: Solid organs and stem cells count matches differently. The classic kidney grade counts HLA-A, B and DR, two each, for six antigens.

For unrelated stem-cell donors, the 2019 NMDP and CIBMTR guideline asks for high-resolution matching at HLA-A, B, C and DRB1: eight of eight. Any single mismatch at these loci lowered survival, and no locus was better tolerated than another.
DPB1 is mismatched in most unrelated transplants, so the aim is a permissive T-cell-epitope mismatch. DQB1 has not been shown on its own to change survival; a ten-of-ten count simply adds DQB1.
Back to the hook: zero two, zero one versus zero two, zero two is a second-field protein difference. If it lies in the antigen recognition domain, the donor is seven of eight.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “The renal 6/6 includes HLA-C and DQ” (✓ the classic 6 = HLA-A, -B, -DR, two each); “A*02:01 vs A*02:02 is a third-field difference” (✓ second field = different protein); “HLA-DP was never serologic, so it does not matter” (✓ DPB1 is typed by DNA and nonpermissive DPB1 mismatches lower survival after unrelated HCT; the 2026 WHO nomenclature report has now also named serologic DP specificities).

cues.text: Trap one: the kidney six-of-six includes HLA-C and DQ. No: the classic six are HLA-A, B and DR, two each.
Trap two: A star zero two, zero one versus zero two, zero two is a third-field difference. No: they differ in the second field, so the proteins differ.
Trap three: DP had no serologic definition, so it does not matter. No: DPB1 is typed by DNA, and nonpermissive DPB1 mismatches lower survival after unrelated stem-cell transplant.

props.title: ✗ “No DP serology, so DP is irrelevant.”

scenes.title: Street, house, paint, garden
scenes.altText: Memory aid: read an allele name like an address. Field 1 = the STREET (allele group); field 2 = the HOUSE (the protein: a different house is a mismatch); field 3 = the PAINT (silent change, same house); field 4 = the GARDEN (outside the coding exons). Tokens: street · house · paint · garden. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: read an allele name like an address. The first field is the street, the second is the house, the third is the paint, and the fourth is the garden. A different house is a different protein: a mismatch.

Where it breaks: a change in the paint or garden can still silence an allele and make it null; matching often counts only the antigen-binding region, so some second-field differences are grouped together; and not every protein mismatch carries equal risk.

props.title: Where it breaks
lines: Paint or garden change can still make a null allele

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Field 1 = group · field 2 = protein · field 3 = silent · field 4 = introns”, “Kidney 6 = A, B, DR · unrelated HCT 8/8 = A, B, C, DRB1 at high resolution + permissive DPB1”.

cues.text: A second-field difference is a protein mismatch, and while kidney matching counts six antigens at HLA-A, B and DR, the unrelated stem-cell donor guideline aims for eight of eight at high resolution for HLA-A, B, C and DRB1, with a matched or permissive DPB1.

props.label: Kidney 6 = A, B, DR · HCT 8/8 = A, B, C, DRB1 + permissive DPB1

explanation.what: Plain language: an HLA allele name is a precise address, and labs can read it at different depths. Classic kidney allocation counts mismatches at three genes; unrelated stem-cell donor matching looks at four genes at high resolution, the level that separates proteins differing in the antigen recognition domain. Scientific terms: allele group (first field), protein (second field, nonsynonymous), synonymous (third field), intron/UTR (fourth field), null (N) and low (L) suffixes, high-resolution (two-field) typing, antigen recognition domain, SSP, SSO, SBT, NGS, phasing, 8/8 match, DPB1 T-cell-epitope (TCE) permissive mismatch.
explanation.why: A second-field difference changes the amino-acid sequence; the antigen recognition domain binds peptides and interacts with T-cell and natural-killer-cell receptors, and in the NMDP/CIBMTR analysis allele-level mismatches lowered survival as much as antigen-level ones. Motif-based PCR methods only find what they look for; sequencing reveals new alleles and resolves ambiguity.
explanation.measure: Kidney: HLA-A, -B, -DR, two each = 6 (reported as mismatches out of 6). Unrelated HCT (NMDP/CIBMTR 2019): type patient and donors by DNA at high resolution for HLA-A, -B, -C, -DRB1 and -DPB1; aim for 8/8 at A, B, C, DRB1; then prefer a matched or permissive DPB1 TCE mismatch; minimise DQB1 and DRB3/4/5 mismatches. DPB1 mismatches occur in more than 80% of unrelated HCT.
explanation.differs: Field 2 (protein) vs field 3 (silent) difference; SSP/SSO (known motifs) vs SBT (exons, two fields) vs NGS (whole gene, phase, beyond two fields); 6-antigen kidney grade vs 8/8 HCT; 8/8 vs “10/10” (adds DQB1).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: name the field in which two alleles differ, choose the method that finds novel alleles, or list the loci in a kidney 6-antigen match versus an HCT 8/8 or 10/10 match.

mnemonic.text: Read an allele name like an address: field 1 is the STREET (allele group), field 2 the HOUSE (protein), field 3 the PAINT (silent change), field 4 the GARDEN (introns and untranslated regions). A different house is a mismatch.
mnemonic.explanation: Separates the protein-changing second field from the silent third and noncoding fourth fields.
mnemonic.limitation: A change outside the second field can still create a null allele; matching often counts only the antigen-binding region, so some second-field differences are grouped as identical; not every protein mismatch carries the same risk.

analogyLimitations: Allele names and cards are schematic.

Match rules shown are the classic kidney grade and the 2019 NMDP/CIBMTR adult unrelated-donor guideline; cord blood units follow separate criteria in the same guideline, and related or haploidentical donors are not covered here.
takeaway: A second-field difference is a protein mismatch, and while kidney matching counts six antigens at HLA-A, B and DR, the unrelated stem-cell donor guideline aims for eight of eight at high resolution for HLA-A, B, C and DRB1, with a matched or permissive DPB1.

questions.stem: A donor types HLA-A*02:01 and the patient types HLA-A*02:02 at that allele. Which statement is correct?

options.text: They differ in the second field, so the encoded proteins differ
options.rationale: Correct. A second-field difference means at least one amino-acid-changing substitution.

options.text: They differ only in the third field, a silent change
options.rationale: Incorrect. The third field would be the next colon-separated number; here the second field differs.

options.text: They differ only in an intron, so they count as a match
options.rationale: Incorrect. Intron or untranslated-region differences are shown in the fourth field.

options.text: They are different allele groups, like A1 versus A2
options.rationale: Incorrect. Both share the first field, 02, the same allele group.

questions.stem: Under the 2019 NMDP/CIBMTR guideline, which loci make up the core “8/8” high-resolution match for an adult unrelated stem-cell donor?

options.rationale: Correct. Two alleles at each of these four loci; any single mismatch was linked to lower survival.
Incorrect. That is the classic six-antigen kidney match grade.
Incorrect. Adding DQB1 gives the “10/10” count; DQB1 has not been shown alone to change survival.
Incorrect. These are class II loci only; DPB1 is handled by choosing a permissive mismatch.

questions.stem: Which HLA typing method can sequence whole genes, determine the phase of heterozygous positions and identify novel alleles beyond two fields?

options.rationale: Correct. NGS sequences whole genes, phases heterozygous positions and resolves beyond two fields, though batching slows it.
Incorrect. SSP detects known motifs only and cannot recognise a novel allele.
Incorrect. SSO gives low-to-intermediate resolution from known probe patterns and cannot detect a novel allele.
Incorrect. Serology gives first-field, low-resolution types and needs viable cells.

claims.text: Four colon-separated fields (group, protein, synonymous, intron/UTR); N = null, L = low expression.
Serology, SSP/SSO, SBT and NGS by resolution, with their limitations and NGS turnaround.
Classic kidney match grade counts HLA-A, -B and -DR, scored out of 6.

8/8 high-resolution A, B, C, DRB1; any single mismatch lowers survival with no locus better tolerated; allele = antigen mismatch; DPB1 permissive TCE; DQB1 not shown alone to affect survival; 10/10 adds DQB1; two fields = high resolution.
DPB1 typed by DNA and nonpermissive mismatches lower survival; 2026 WHO report names serologic DP specificities.
Reviewer’s 5-year graft-survival figures (~95/88/83%), “single HLA-C mismatches hurt engraftment”, “HLA-A mismatches have the largest impact” and SSP as the deceased-donor method.
claims.note: Not taught; no open source read in this session confirmed them, and Dehn 2019 contradicts the HLA-A claim.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 50 Hit 10 frames HCT matching as “10 of 10” (adding DQB1) and says HLA-A mismatches have the largest impact on GVHD and survival. The 2019 NMDP/CIBMTR guideline (Dehn 2019) uses 8/8 at A, B, C and DRB1 as the core standard, found no locus better tolerated than another, says DQB1 has not been shown in isolation to affect survival, and recommends DPB1 typing with permissive TCE mismatches (register rv-hct-locus-impact).

Ch. 50 Trap 3 says HLA-DP was never defined serologically. DP specificities were historically cellularly defined (DPw), but the 2026 WHO nomenclature report names serologic DPA and DPB specificities (register rv-dp-serology). The trap’s main point, that DP matters for HCT, stands.
